body.text: India and China share a long and multi-layered history of cultural, economic, and civilisational relations that go back to ancient trade routes and the spread of Buddhism. In recent times, their interdependence has gone through various stages of cooperation, rivalry, and strategic caution. Since the early 2000s, bilateral economic relations have deepened, with China becoming India's largest trading partner in 2008,[1] and thereafter competing with the United States (US) to retain that position. That trade, however, is highly uneven, and India’s trade deficit peaked in 2025-26 at US$99.21 billion, due to heavy Indian imports of Chinese electronic components, electrical machinery, industrial machinery, and telecommunications equipment.[2]

Both countries are part of several multilateral settings. They cooperate in organisations such as BRICS, begun in 2009, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), incorporated in 2016, and the New Development Bank (NDB), started in 2014, of which both countries are founding members. Though India has not endorsed China’s flagship Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), since the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) passes through Pakistan Occupied Kashmir (POK),[3] it has been careful in spelling out its position. Both countries have worked together as part of the G20 framework, notably during India's G20 presidency in 2023, and also as members of the World Health Organization (WHO), where, at the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccine diplomacy issues created tensions between them.

This intricate web of cooperation and competition underscores the need for India to study China closely—its strategic objectives, economic models, and policy processes. Understanding these will help India make better policy choices, especially in a world of multipolarity and technological dislocation.

The Galwan Valley face-off between the Indian and Chinese armies, which began on 6 May 2020 and simmered for months, was of crucial importance for India-China relations. It was also a turning point for China studies in India. For the first time in over 30 years, bloodshed at the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in June 2020, unleashed a rapid transformation of public sentiment and government policy towards China, and led as well to a re-orientation of academic enquiry. Educational exchanges between the two countries reduced, with memorandums of understanding (MoUs) between Indian and Chinese universities, both those already signed and others at the discussion stage, requiring clearances from India’s Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) and Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). Both India and China curtailed visa access for scholars and journalists; India increased its scrutiny of collaborations with Chinese institutions, and, above all, China studies in India changed from an interdisciplinary field with various perspectives to a narrowly-defined field focusing on military strategy and border security issues framed within a context of geopolitical rivalry.

This change has narrowed the scope and reduced the independence of the knowledge ecosystem on China. Information has become less accessible, and fieldwork less feasible. Bureaucratic and institutional limitations, along with paucity of funding, of institutional autonomy and research infrastructure, further inhibit scholars. As a result, vis-à-vis China, India's strategic community and policy world is becoming increasingly reliant on secondary sources, often produced in the West.

This academic disengagement has occurred at a most critical time. China and India will soon become the world's largest economies, apart from the United States. India's ability to engage with China, whether in terms of diplomacy, trade, or security, will be closely tied to knowledge systems. China's unrestrained investment in infrastructure, manufacturing, and innovative technological developments, particularly through initiatives like the BRI, has fundamentally altered the pillars of regional and global geopolitics and supply chain systems. India needs to respond intelligently to these transformations, based on fundamental research and historical knowledge.

The India-China economic relationship has continued to grow despite political tensions. This economic interdependence, primarily due to the flow of Chinese machinery, electronics, and intermediate goods into India, alongside India’s narrow, raw materials-focused export basket, presents risks for India's long-term development, national security goals, and economic planning process. Managing the challenges requires strategic policy changes and a nuanced understanding of the Chinese economy, regulatory frameworks, and industrial policies. India needs to examine China’s growth trajectory through a focused, evidence-based, and interdisciplinary lens.

This report is in six parts, with this first part contextualising the need for India to undertake studies of China. The second part traces the historical evolution of China studies in India from early cultural engagement and hopeful beginnings through a security-centric phase beginning with the India-China war of 1962, through an era of research growth propelled by liberalisation, and finally, the backtracking and securitisation that followed Galwan. The third segment highlights the thematic areas discussed in the Indian literature on China before and after Galwan. The fourth section focuses on the institutional and structural weaknesses of China studies in India; the fifth highlights recommendations; and the final segment stresses certain conclusions.
China studies in India have evolved through distinct phases, shaped by geopolitical shifts, economic transformations, and changing academic priorities.

In the pre-British empire days, China-India contacts were mainly cultural and religious. Buddhism was the biggest link between the two civilisations, carried from India to China along both the Silk Route and through the sea trade. Chinese monks Faxian (5th century CE) and Xuanzang (7th century CE) visited India and wrote about Indian society, its economy, and its religious institutions.

Under British rule in India, China was analysed primarily to serve British strategic and commercial interests, and not as an academic subject in its own right. British India’s main concerns were the opium trade, geopolitical issues relating to Tibet, and Chinese immigration to colonial port cities such as Calcutta and Bombay. There was little or no formal academic study of China from an India perspective.

Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru’s vision emphasised Asian solidarity and cooperation, viewing China as a natural partner in shaping a post-colonial, non-aligned world. This optimism was reflected in the 1954 Panchsheel Agreement between Nehru and Chinese Prime Minister Zhou En Lai, which outlined five principles: mutual respect for each other’s territorial integrity and sovereignty, mutual non-aggression, mutual non-interference in each other’s internal affairs, mutual benefit and equality, and peaceful coexistence.[4]

It was during this phase that China-related studies were started at institutions like Delhi University and Visva-Bharati University (Santiniketan, West Bengal), and discussions on China's role in the non-aligned movement (NAM) began. Even so, structured China studies did not develop in India to the same extent that India studies did in China; India still did not have specialised centres for the study of the Chinese economy, society, and domestic politics. With the Sino-Indian War of October-November 1962, all relations came to a standstill and institutional research on China came to an end. Indian studies on China became largely security driven, focused on the border conflict, military strategies, and China’s role in global geopolitics.[5],[6]

The Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (IDSA) in Delhi, set up in 1965, was one of the earliest Indian institutions studying China and particularly focused on defence and strategic affairs. During this phase, Indian scholars had limited access to China and remained dependent on secondary sources, especially Western think tanks and intelligence reports. Due to travel restrictions, they had no direct exposure to China. As a result, vital developments in China, such as the Cultural Revolution (1966-76) and Deng Xiaoping's economic reforms (1978-1990), could not be extensively studied in India.[7]

Although trade, on a very limited scale, was resumed with China in 1978, the breakthrough in diplomatic relations came with then Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi’s visit to China in December 1988. As political scientist Kanti Bajpai has noted: “From 1988 onwards, India-China relations came to rest on four pillars that undergirded a fair degree of military and diplomatic stability: summitry, border negotiations, confidence-building measures, and people-to-people ties, including trade."[8]
This comprised the following:
Summitry: A chain of high-level meetings that followed between the top leadership of China and India at bilateral and multilateral levels, promoting direct dialogue and mitigating tensions.
Border negotiations: Discussions intended to secure peace along the disputed India-China borders, seeking to facilitate conflict resolution.

Confidence-building measures: Agreements and mechanisms designed to lessen misunderstandings and obviate conflicts, such as border military communications, military tasking protocols, and agreements regulating the movement of peacekeeping forces of both countries along the borders.

People-to-people engagements: Aimed at improving educational, cultural, and economic ties. Since then, these interconnections of trade, education, and even tourism have led to a better understanding between the two nations and promoted economic integration.

India’s economic liberalisation in 1991 transformed its relationship with China. The two countries fully normalised diplomatic ties, leading to renewed interest in India in China’s economic model, trade policies, and industrial strategies. This phase of global cooperation can be divided into two periods:

The first decade (1991-2000) saw initial engagement and institutional expansion of China studies. With the rapid economic rise of China becoming a significant research topic, think tanks such as the Institute of Chinese Studies (ICS), Delhi, and Jawaharlal Nehru University's Centre for East Asian Studies expanded their focus on contemporary China. However, scholarly interest in China was still largely confined to elite institutions, with limited integration of China studies into mainstream Indian universities.[9]

During the second period (2001-2020), institutional involvement increased. India and China became economically interdependent, leading to considerable research into China's supply chains, digital economy, and contribution to global governance. Think tanks such as the Observer Research Foundation (ORF), IDSA, ICS, and Brookings India started researching China's BRI, its strides in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and 5G telecom technology, and the impact of China's emergence on India. MoUs between Chinese and Indian universities, which included both research and language learning programmes, increased. Confucius Institutes set up in India (funded by the Chinese government, as part of its global cultural outreach) provided Mandarin training, increasing Indian scholars' access to Chinese primary sources.[10],[11]

At informal summits in Wuhan, China (April 2018) and Mamallapuram, Tamil Nadu (October 2019), Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping sought to further normalise bilateral relations and intensify cooperation in the economic, technological, cultural, and political spheres. However, India’s security and strategic concerns have also limited the cooperation. On 1 October 2019, for instance, just before the Mamallapuram summit, India’s University Grants Commission (UGC) mandated that educational institutions should seek prior approval of both the Home and External Affairs ministries for any academic cooperation with Chinese universities. It shows that even before the Galwan clash, India’s approach to engagement with Chinese academia had become cautious.[12]

Until 2020, there were seven Confucius Institutes/classrooms in different parts of India, and 54 agreements between Indian and Chinese universities to engage in educational and cultural exchanges. But following the Galwan Valley clashes, India suspended all MoUs with Chinese universities, halting joint research projects and Confucius Institutes’ Mandarin language classes. Further, Mandarin was removed from the Central Board of Secondary Education's (CBSE) list of foreign languages[13] Indian school students could pursue. Once again, visa restrictions made field research in China nearly impossible, forcing scholars to rely on secondary data.[14],[15]

The absence of first-hand engagement has again increased reliance on Western perspectives, limiting India's ability to analyse China's domestic changes independently. Fortunately, developments since 2024–25, such as discussions on restoring people-to-people exchanges and easing of travel restrictions, suggest a cautious reopening of avenues for academic interaction. Whether these translate into a broader revival of China studies in India remains to be seen.

Academic research since Galwan has become overwhelmingly focused on military, cybersecurity, and geostrategic aspects, particularly on China's role in the Indo-Pacific, the Quad, and China’s military modernisation. While China-India trade have risen, research on China’s industrial policies, trade practices, and innovation strategies has declined.[16],[17] Conducting objective research and interacting with Chinese scholars and institutions have become sensitive matters. Visas, academic collaborations, and people-to-people exchanges remain restricted. Funding of Chinese language education and China studies in India has also reduced.

In the coming years, the challenge for Indian academia will be balancing the study of strategic issues with in-depth research, to ensure that India has a comprehensive picture of China's role in the world.

Between 2000 and 2020, China studies in India diversified beyond the traditionally dominant themes of military strategy and security concerns. Scholars began to view China as an economic force whose policies and growth trajectories had profound implications for India and the global order. The rise of China's economy,[18] particularly following its accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2001, attracted much scholarly attention. This period saw a surge in research focusing on China's economic reforms, trade policies, industrial strategies, and technological advancements, creating a more multi-dimensional approach to China studies.

By the first decade of 2000s, China's rapid urbanisation and infrastructure development had also become a focus for Indian scholars studying urban governance and smart city initiatives. Comparative studies of Indian and Chinese urban models emerged, particularly focused on China's Special Economic Zones and their role in driving industrial growth. Indian policymakers looked toward China's manufacturing and export-led growth model, prompting research on supply chain management, trade competitiveness, and the role of state-owned enterprises in China's industrial policy.[19] This period also witnessed a growing focus on China's innovation ecosystem, with scholars analysing its rise in information technology (IT), artificial intelligence (AI), and digital platforms. Indian research institutions and think tanks such as the ICS, ORF, and the Centre for East Asian Studies at JNU played key roles in advancing research on China's economic policies and digital economy.

The launch of China's BRI in 2013 further accelerated research in India on China's global ambitions and their likely impact on South Asia. Indian scholars analysed China's infrastructure diplomacy, investment patterns, and geopolitical influence across Asia and Africa. The debate over India's response to the BRI led to extensive research on China's soft power, its role in multilateral institutions, and its strategic use of economic tools for geopolitical leverage.[20] Indian think tanks such as IDSA and ORF produced policy reports assessing the impact of China's growing presence in the Indian Ocean region, its engagement in African economies, and its evolving global governance strategy.

During this period, both India’s MEA and China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also sought to facilitate cooperation and linkages between Indian and Chinese cities, states and provinces. They signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on 20 May 2013 to facilitate closer cooperation between local authorities in India and China,[21] leading to 24 agreements by May 2015—these spanned New Delhi and Beijing, Bengaluru and Chengdu, Kolkata and Kunming, Mumbai and Shanghai, Chennai and Chongqing, Hyderabad and Qingdao, and even Aurangabad and Dunhuang.[22],[23] The city councils agreed to cooperate on education, culture, sports, youth affairs, urban planning, waste water management, infrastructure, environment, public health, and trade.[24] However, what came of these agreements remains largely under-researched.

In this phase, direct academic engagement between Indian and Chinese institutions peaked. Universities and research centres collaborated through formal agreements, facilitating student and faculty exchanges, joint conferences, and collaborative research projects. Mandarin language programmes expanded across Indian universities, with the Confucius Institutes playing a key role. Scholars conducting fieldwork in China benefited from first-hand exposure to China's economic and political structures, enabling richer and more nuanced analyses.[25]

To be sure, even during this interlude, China studies in India faced structural challenges. The lack of widespread Chinese language proficiency among Indian scholars remained a hurdle. Many scholars continued to rely on secondary sources in English rather than engage with Chinese primary materials. Research was also still concentrated in a few elite institutions, with limited penetration into India's broader academic landscape.

The 2020 Galwan Valley clash saw academic exchanges and joint initiatives that were a hallmark of the previous two decades severely curtailed. Several MoUs between Indian and Chinese institutions were suspended and obtaining research visas became difficult, effectively stopping direct engagement. Once again, as in the post 1962-conflict years, primary data collection became challenging. Joint conferences and intuitional collaborations reduced due to the geopolitical uncertainty, further exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The focus of China studies moved firmly to securitisation—the border dispute, China’s military modernisation, cybersecurity, and the overall geopolitical competition—while China’s economic policies, industrial development, and digital economy, received less attention. Indian scholars became wary of interaction with Chinese academic institutions, lest they be subject to investigation or criticism.

A scan of the recent publications indexed in the global citation database Scopus confirms that China studies in India has not declined excessively following Galwan, but has been reoriented, with themes such as the Indo-Pacific, supply-chain resilience, technological transformation, China and the Taiwan Strait, the role of China in the new world order and global governance, receiving growing attention. But this has also been changing since 2024, as diplomatic relations with China have started normalising and economic engagement has spiked. China studies too, is once again moving beyond the traditional security field.

China studies in India have faced multiple institutional and structural hurdles. These vary from shortage of funds and institutional disorganisation, to lack of access, to primary data and linguistic challenges. The following paragraphs discuss the biggest impediments:

India's China studies ecosystem is not as developed as that of the West. Institutions such as the Centre for East Asian Studies (JNU), the ICS, and IDSA have contributed to the discourse on China, but they remain constrained by limited resources, shortage of faculty, and lack of continued financial support from the government or private enterprise. Western universities often have a long history of research on China, and well-established funding streams, endowments and government supported research grants that enable long-term, in-depth work on China. Indian institutions depend on ad-hoc government funding and short-term projects.

This lack of consistent funding means that China research in India is often reactive rather than proactive, focused on immediate security concerns or geopolitical crises rather than long-term strategic research on China's economic, technological, and societal transformations. Further, limited funding opportunities make young scholars reluctant to specialise in China studies, fearing it will not help their academic careers. This leads to a shallow China studies academic pipeline for the next generation of China experts in India.

A critical factor limiting India's China scholarship is lack of direct engagement with China through field-based research. Before the Galwan clash, academic exchanges and research visits to China enabled Indian scholars to engage directly with Chinese institutions, policymakers, businesses, and researchers. Field visits provided invaluable insights into China's political economy, industrial policies, urban governance, and technological advancements. However, post-Galwan, academic visits to China have been almost entirely halted, as China has denied visas, cutting off Indian researchers from direct access to primary sources. [26]

This has led to an overreliance on secondary sources, including media reports and think tank publications from Western countries. While these are useful, they often reflect external perspectives shaped by geopolitical priorities that may not always align with India's interests. The absence of first-hand data collection weakens the originality and depth of research, making it difficult for Indian scholars to produce independent analyses of China's policies.[27]

As noted earlier, India too, has imposed restrictions on academic collaborations with Chinese institutions. It has become difficult for scholars to engage in joint research projects, access Chinese academic databases, or even participate in online conferences with their Chinese counterparts.[28]

India lacks enough scholars with a high level of Chinese language proficiency. In the West, there are numerous scholars who speak fluent Mandarin and communicate directly with Chinese sources, but many Indian researchers rely on translated material, that might contain biases or lack nuance.[29]

Since national security concerns, understandably, take precedence over academic engagement, the Confucius Institutes and Confucius Classrooms in the country have also been subjected to greater scrutiny since bilateral relations soured in 2020. They have been comprehensively examined by the government, to the extent that the Chinese Embassy officially requested India to do so in an “objective and fair manner”, and cautioned against politicising academic exchanges. The review, which examined institutional transparency, was motivated by national security and foreign influence concerns, but these concerns also limited the opportunities for Mandarin language learning in India.

However, the demand for courses in the Chinese language did not reduce. Instead, more and more private language institutes, internet-based language learning tools, extension programmes at universities, and special language training facilities for students, businessmen and job seekers associated with China, have taken over from the Confucius Institutes.

China-Japan tensions, which include two bitter wars, run much deeper than the India-China hostility—yet Japan has never restricted Mandarin language learning, nor has China clamped down on Japanese. Both countries have persisted in developing independent centres of excellence and area studies programmes, along with Mandarin language training at universities, which the governments continue to finance. Similarly, for all its geopolitical tensions with China, the US government continues to support institutions like the Fairbank Centre for Chinese Studies, Harvard University, or the Stanford Centre on China's Economy and Institutions at Stanford University. Australia maintains a high quality Centre on China in the World at the Australian National University. These countries realise that deeper knowledge of China, not less, equips them better in their strategic rivalry with China. The US’s Title VI National Resource Centres[30],[31],[32],[33] provide grants to universities teaching foreign languages, including Mandarin. India could learn from their example.

Without adequate knowledge of Mandarin, India's capacity to interpret China's policies is bound to be hampered. Indian scholars may miss key details in official Chinese documents. It is thus essential to develop a cadre of experts capable of engaging in direct policy dialogue with Chinese counterparts. India needs to start new, independent Mandarin language programmes within Indian universities, free from political influences. It should develop indigenous and institutionally autonomous Mandarin-language training capacities that are less dependent on externally supported programmes.

Another emerging challenge in China studies in India is the increasing pressure to align research with nationalistic narratives. While it is essential to examine China's policies critically, the growing influence of ideological positions in academia has sometimes limited objective analysis and critical engagement. The securitisation of China studies has led to a disproportionate focus on military and strategic issues, sidelining research on China's economic transformation, technological advancements, and governance models. [34]

Scholars researching non-security aspects of China often face scrutiny, with concerns that their engagement with Chinese sources or institutions points to their being overly sympathetic to China. This has led to self-censorship in academia, where researchers may avoid certain topics or limit their engagement with Chinese academic material to avoid being seen as politically controversial. The narrowing of research themes reduces intellectual diversity and weakens India's ability to develop a comprehensive understanding of China beyond immediate security concerns.[35]

Further, the lack of space for independent, critical debate has weakened the overall quality of scholarship. A robust China studies ecosystem requires varied perspectives, rigorous peer review, and the ability to question dominant narratives. In contrast, the increasing politicisation of China studies has led to a constrained intellectual environment, where particular viewpoints are privileged over others.[36]

The institutional and structural weaknesses of China studies in India are bound to affect the country's ability to formulate informed policies on China. The fragmented and underfunded research ecosystem, lack of field-based research and primary data access, closure of Mandarin language programmes, and growing securitisation of academic discourse, have collectively weakened India's China expertise. If India is to develop a sophisticated and independent China studies ecosystem, it must address these structural issues.[37]

Without a comprehensive strategy to strengthen China studies, India risks being unable to effectively analyse and respond to China's economic, technological, and geopolitical rise. A long-term vision that fosters independent, data-driven, and globally competitive China research is crucial to ensure that India remains an active and informed participant in regional and global affairs.

A balanced system is needed that ensures national security considerations are met while also providing the resources to study one of India’s most important neighbours and a potential superpower. A sustainable and independent ecosystem for China studies calls for the following:

The number of courses teaching Mandarin must be increased to reduce reliance on translated material and Western interpretations of developments in China. Universities with established expertise, such as JNU, Banaras Hindu University, University of Delhi, Central University of Gujarat, and University of Mumbai, should get adequate governmental funding to enhance their Chinese language training and translation programmes. A larger pool of scholars capable of directly engaging with Chinese primary sources is required for independent and evidence-based research.

China studies should not be focused exclusively on security and include more interdisciplinary research. Funding mechanisms should be created to support research on China’s economy, industrial policy, urbanisation, government practices, technological innovation, environmental policies, demographic changes, and social transformation. A broader research agenda will provide policymakers with a deeper understanding of the different facets of China’s rise and its implications for India.

Recognising that the current geopolitical realities limit opportunities for direct academic and collaborative engagement between Indian and Chinese academic institutions, India should work to strengthen alternative knowledge networks through partnerships with research centres and universities in Taiwan, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Australia, and Europe. Collaborating with these countries will allow access to research, training opportunities, and comparative perspectives on China while safeguarding strategic interests.

Institutions such as the UGC, the Indian Council of Social Science Research (ICSSR), in partnership with the MEA, could establish a dedicated research programme on China studies. It should include funding for doctoral fellowships, post-doctoral research, faculty exchanges, translation projects, and long-term field-based research. Funding needs to be predictable and stable to develop a new cadre of China specialists over time.

As part of this process, the MEA can establish designated China Studies Chairs in universities and other institutions that conduct research on China. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, for instance, has set up more than 25 Chairs under the Dr Ambedkar Foundation, setting themes for each of these Chairs. The Chairs could work as centres of excellence for teaching, research, policy dialogue, and public outreach, addressing contemporary issues associated with China, India and the global order. The Chairs would be able to support visiting scholars, conduct research projects, hold annual conferences and roundtables, have continuous lecture series, conduct publication programmes, and connect researchers working on China to their counterparts, both in India and across the globe. Such Chairs, held by people with pre-existing expertise, would work towards establishing a distributed, geographically and institutionally sustainable China studies ecosystem in India.

India must develop stronger institutional mechanisms to collect, analyse, and disseminate information related to China. It should provide support to think tanks, universities, and research institutions to encourage the development of independent databases, policy repositories, and sources of information related to China in areas such as economics, technology, and politics. Reducing India's reliance on secondary information and externally mediated interpretations will enable the development of high-quality, context-based, and policy-relevant knowledge on China.

India needs to develop a unified digital repository for research on China, comprising datasets, translation, policy documents, and archive materials related to China. It could be jointly managed by the UGC, the ICSSR, the MEA, and key research institutions. Such a repository would facilitate distribution of knowledge about China through greater cooperation among universities, think tanks, government agencies, and individual researchers, while reducing duplication of work. It would also improve availability of primary sources from China as well as Chinese language translations of documents, policy reports, and scholarly publications.

Ultimately, India needs a balanced approach vis-à-vis China that places equal emphasis on national security concerns and long-term development of academic expertise. Building institutional capacity, encouraging independent scholarship, and fostering language proficiency is critical to ensuring that India possesses the knowledge infrastructure necessary to engage with China in an increasingly complex global environment.

The transformation of Chinese studies in India is indicative of the overall evolution of India-China relations. It has adapted to shifting global political structures: from early civilisational encounters to post-1947 idealism, to post-1962 security-focused China relations, and now a more varied method of researching China, reflecting the changing geopolitical landscape Academic exchanges and other developments between 2000 and 2020 marked its most dynamic phase, with many new institutions being established, increasing numbers of academic exchanges between India and China, widespread increase of Indians learning Mandarin, and a much broader research agenda embracing China’s economy, technology, and governance and global issues.

Since the post-Galwan period, however, these developments have been reoriented. Academic exchanges between India and China have decreased, access to empirical field work in China is now much more difficult, and increasingly, China studies has come to focus primarily on strategic/security concerns. At the same time, this has also been a period when the importance of strengthening and enhancing scholarly engagement, and independent interdisciplinary research on China, has increased. The scope and availability of China studies in India should be widened, which will enable an in-depth understanding of China's domestic developments, industrial strategies, ambitions for high technology, governance systems, and international engagement.

As India seeks to develop enhanced strategic autonomy, economic resilience, and a key role in an increasingly multipolar world, developing high-quality, evidence-based, and India-specific knowledge of China, will be a key element of national capability. Building that capability is not just an academic activity but also a strategic investment, which will support evidence-based policymaking and successful diplomacy.
